'''Herman Otto Hartley''' (born Hermann Otto Hirschfeld in [[Berlin]], [[Germany]]; 1912–1980) was a [[German American]] [[statistician]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=H. O. Hartley (1912–1980)|first=William|last=Smith|url=https://magazine.amstat.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/hartleyho.pdf|journal=Amstat News|date=September 2005|pages=10-11}}</ref> He made significant contributions in many areas of statistics, mathematical programming, and optimization. He also founded [[Texas A&M University]]'s Department of Statistics.

Hartley's earliest papers appeared under the name H.O. Hirschfeld. He translated his German last name Hirschfeld (Hirsch = Hart, Feld = field = lea = ley) into English.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=David |first=H.A. |title=H.O. Hartley, 1912–1980 |journal=[[International Statistical Review]] |volume=50 |pages=327–330 |jstor=1402502 |number=3}}</ref>

== Career ==
In 1934, at the age of 22, Hartley earned a Ph.D. in mathematics from the [[Humboldt University of Berlin|University of Berlin]], followed by a Ph.D. in mathematical statistics from the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1940 and a Doctorate of Science in mathematical statistics from [[University College London]] in 1954.<ref name="mathgene">{{MathGenealogy|id=20670}}</ref> He began his independent academic career at UCL, where he met [[Egon Pearson]], with whom he collaborated to produce the classic two-volume ''Biometrika Tables for Statisticians,'' and also developed [[Hartley's test|Hartley's F-max test]]<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Hartley|first=H. O.|date=1950|title=The Maximum F-Ratio as a Short-Cut Test for Heterogeneity of Variance|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/2332383|journal=Biometrika|volume=37|issue=3/4|pages=308–312|doi=10.2307/2332383|jstor=2332383 |pmid=14801057 |issn=0006-3444|url-access=subscription}}</ref> for equality of variances.

A one-year Visiting Research Professor in Statistics position at then-[[Iowa State College]] brought Hartley to the United States in 1953.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Smith|first=W.B.|date=August 1981|title=In Memoriam: Herman Otto Hartley (1912–1980)|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2683980|journal=[[The American Statistician]]|volume=35|issue=3 |pages=142–143|doi=10.1080/00031305.1981.10479332 |jstor=2683980 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> The position was extended after that initial year to include nine more years, during which he became involved in research and teaching. He was involved in instituting computing both for scientific and administrative purposes at Iowa State, which for the first time had university-wide service in data processing and numerical analysis. He also was a consultant on statistics to a wide variety of scientists on campus.{{cn|date=November 2025}}

After a decade at Iowa State, Hartley moved to Texas A&M University, where he was appointed in 1963 as a distinguished professor and founding director of the Institute of Statistics.<ref name=":0">{{cite book | editor-last1=Agresti | editor-first1=Alan | editor-last2=Meng | editor-first2=Xiao-Li | title=Strength in Numbers: The Rising of Academic Statistics Departments in the U. S. | publisher=Springer | publication-place=New York | date=2012 | isbn=978-1-4614-3648-5 }}</ref> He led the Graduate Institute of Statistics, which had been formed a year earlier. In the ensuing decade and a half, he built his initial faculty of four into a group of 16, directed more than 30 doctoral students, and attracted significant research funding.{{cn|date=November 2025}}

Hartley remained active at Texas A&M until 1979, when he accepted a full-time visiting professor position at [[Duke University]] while also serving as statistician with the National Testing Service in Durham, N.C., until his death on December 30, 1980.

Hartley was an elected fellow of the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]] (1949) and the [[American Statistical Association]] (1953)<ref>{{cite journal|date=February 1954|title=Election of New Fellows|journal=[[The American Statistician]]|volume=8|issue=1|pages=17–18|doi=10.1080/00031305.1954.10482018|jstor=2681662}}</ref> as well as an elected member of the [[International Statistical Institute]] (1954). He served as president of the Eastern North American Region of the Biometric Society (1959), which was the first region formed in the present-day [[International Biometric Society]], and as president of the American Statistical Association (1979). Hartley earned the ASA's 1973 [[Wilks Memorial Award]] recognizing his national and international efforts in the field of statistics.

== Research ==
Hartley published nearly 100 papers (three-quarters of them during the final two decades of his career) in top-tiered journals until his mandatory retirement in 1977.

Hartley's most well-known work includes:
* ''Biometrika Tables for Statisticians'' with E. Pearson in 1954 and 1972
* The origination of the [[EM Algorithm]] methodology while at Iowa State in 1958.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Hartley |first1=H. O. |last2=Rao |first2=J. N. K. |date=1967 |title=Maximum-Likelihood Estimation for the Mixed Analysis of Variance Model |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/2333854 |journal=Biometrika |volume=54 |issue=1/2 |pages=93–108 |doi=10.2307/2333854 |jstor=2333854 |pmid=6049561 |issn=0006-3444|url-access=subscription }}</ref>  Today it is one of the most widely used estimation methods.
* [[Hartley's test|Hartley's F-max Test for equality of variances]]<ref name=":1" />

He also made contributions to:
* Politz-Simmons Estimator, which is a method for dealing with bias due to "not at home" entries in survey sampling.
* Hartley-Ross Estimator, which aims to estimate the mean of finite population of size N with the help of a known mean of a correlated variable. Unbiasedness proved and variance given.
* RHC Sampling Scheme, which estimates the population total using an unequal-probability sampling without replacement from a finite population
* [[Correspondence analysis]], which is similar to principal component analysis but as applied to [[categorical variable|categorical data]].

Hartley's other research spanned a variety of topics, including:
* Sample survey estimation and design<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hartley  |first1=H. O. |last2=Rao |first2=J. N. K. |date=1968 |title=A new estimation theory for sample surveys |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/biomet/55.3.547 |journal=Biometrika |volume=55 |issue=3 |pages=547–557 |doi=10.1093/biomet/55.3.547 |issn=0006-3444|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* Mathematical optimization<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hartley |first=H. O. |date=1961 |title=Nonlinear Programming by the Simplex Method |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/1909291 |journal=Econometrica |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=223–237 |doi=10.2307/1909291 |jstor=1909291 |issn=0012-9682|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hartley |first1=H. O. |last2=Hocking |first2=R. R. |date=1963 |title=Convex Programming by Tangential Approximation |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.9.4.600 |journal=Management Science |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=600–612 |doi=10.1287/mnsc.9.4.600 |issn=0025-1909|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* Variance component estimation<ref name=":2" />
* Stochastic PERT<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hartley |first1=H. O. |last2=Wortham |first2=A. W. |date=1966 |title=A Statistical Theory for PERT Critical Path Analysis |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.12.10.b469 |journal=Management Science |volume=12 |issue=10 |pages=B-469–B-481 |doi=10.1287/mnsc.12.10.b469 |issn=0025-1909|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* The development of designed experiments to estimate safe doses of carcinogenic agents

== Legacy ==
Hartley's legacy at Texas A&M includes the H.O. Hartley Award presented annually for the past 40 years to a statistics former student who best reflects Hartley's tradition of distinguished service to the discipline, the biannual Hartley Memorial Lecture Series also named in his honor, and the H.O. Hartley Chair in Statistics,<ref>{{Citation|title=Hartley Endowed Chair Award Ceremony – October 23, 2020| date=23 February 2021 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0VxYD6A3fgs |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211212/0VxYD6A3fgs| archive-date=2021-12-12 |url-status=live|language=en|access-date=2021-06-04}}{{cbignore}}</ref> established in July 2019 by his students and the Thomas W. Powell '62 Endowed Graduate Fellowship Fund.
